claim: A human observer in low Earth orbit has seen the Great Wall of China with the unaided eye.
scope: Verified unaided-eye sighting from low Earth orbit (about 160-420 km; crewed orbital flight such as the ISS). Only Q-exist-ver from C009 v3 (f99c5639 r1). Separate predicates (never visible; easy to see; usually seen; at least one astronaut has reported it) are not answered by this record. Photographs, including long-lens photographs, are not unaided sightings.
answer: The sources reviewed do not establish whether anyone has seen the Great Wall from low Earth orbit with the unaided eye. NASA describes it as difficult or impossible to see from orbit without high-powered lenses, and says it generally is not visible to the unaided eye from low Earth orbit; ESA astronaut Thomas Pesquet wrote that it cannot be seen from space, though he photographed it with a 1150 mm lens. Some astronauts have been reported as saying they saw it, but none of those reports is verified here as an unaided sighting. This is an abstention on the evidence, not a finding that it is impossible.

evidence.document: Great Wall of China from space (image caption quoting Thomas Pesquet)
evidence.edition: Web page as retrieved; 2021 per URL path

evidence.statement_type: attributed general guidance plus description of photography

evidence.aid_status: unaided implied by contrast with high-powered lenses
evidence.observation: NASA states the Wall is difficult or impossible to see from Earth orbit without the high-powered lenses used for the photo.
evidence.short_excerpt: difficult or impossible to see from Earth orbit without the high-powered lenses used for this photo

evidence.source_modality: agency blog citing a 2005 NASA story and a 2008 Scientific American article
evidence.aid_status: about astronauts seeing; unaided implied, not explicit
evidence.locator: Paragraph citing 'this NASA story explained in 2005 and this Scientific American story detailed in 2008'
evidence.observation: States the Wall is quite difficult for astronauts to see because of low colour contrast with surrounding vegetation. Depends on S4 and S8.
evidence.short_excerpt: the Great Wall is quite difficult for astronauts (either in orbit or on the moon) to see

evidence.document: China's Wall Less Great in View from Space (feature, 9 May 2005; PDF capture dated 7/2/2019 of the archived page)
evidence.edition: PDF capture; page last updated 30 November 2007
evidence.source_modality: agency feature article quoting NASA's chief scientist for Earth observation (Kamlesh Lulla)
evidence.statement_type: institutional assessment plus attributed expert statements
evidence.locator: Page 1, opening paragraph; page 2, Lulla quotation and following sentence
evidence.observation: States the Wall generally is not visible to the unaided eye in low Earth orbit, and that it is questionable whether it can be seen with the unaided eye from space. Also reports Leroy Chiao said he did not see the wall when photographing it. Keeps unaided visibility uncertain rather than ruled out.
evidence.short_excerpt: generally isn't, at least to the unaided eye in low Earth orbit

evidence.source_modality: wire report relaying a CCTV interview (Yang Liwei) and quoting the book ORBIT (Apt, Helfert, Wilkinson)
evidence.locator: Yang quotation paragraph; ORBIT quotation paragraph
evidence.observation: Yang Liwei is quoted as saying he did not see the Great Wall; the ORBIT authors wrote they spent several passes looking for it with no luck. Neither says whether the attempt was unaided. Not unaided trials.
evidence.short_excerpt: But I didn't see the Great Wall.

evidence.publisher: NBC News, source Space.com (Robert Roy Britt)
evidence.document: What can you really see from space?
evidence.source_modality: news article quoting astronaut Ed Lu during ISS Expedition 7
evidence.statement_type: attributed report of seeing, with reporter paraphrase
evidence.locator: Paragraph beginning 'So what about the Great Wall of China?' and the following weather paragraph
evidence.observation: Only 'You can see the Great Wall' is inside quotation marks as Lu's words. 'But it's less visible than a lot of other objects. And you have to know where to look.' is the reporter's sentence. The next paragraph says Lu is trying to photograph it and the weather has not cooperated. Aid status and medium not stated.
evidence.short_excerpt: “You can see the Great Wall,” Lu says.

evidence.document: Great Wall not visible from space: official
evidence.source_modality: news article relaying a Straits Times quotation of Gene Cernan
evidence.statement_type: attributed report of seeing, second hand
evidence.locator: Paragraph beginning 'This is not the end of the matter.'
evidence.observation: Cernan is quoted, via the Straits Times, as saying that from Earth orbit of 160-320 km the Wall is visible to the naked eye. Two hops from the speaker; the Straits Times original was not read.
evidence.short_excerpt: the Great Wall of China is indeed visible to the naked eye

evidence.document: Is China's Great Wall Visible from Space?
evidence.source_modality: magazine article with direct quotation (Jeffrey Hoffman) and unsourced paraphrase (Cernan, Lu)
evidence.statement_type: direct quotation of an unsuccessful observer; publisher synthesis
evidence.aid_status: Hoffman: not stated; Cernan/Lu paraphrase: not stated
evidence.locator: Hoffman quotation paragraph; paragraph beginning 'Some U.S. astronauts, notably Eugene Cernan and Ed Lu'
evidence.observation: Hoffman says he never saw the wall despite numerous flights over China. The article also says, without a source, that Cernan and Lu have said they saw it from low orbit and that it shows only in certain lighting; that paraphrase adds nothing independent to S6 or S7 and is not counted.

direct_source_statements: S2 and S4 (NASA) assess unaided visibility from orbit as difficult or impossible, generally absent, and questionable.
S6 and S7 report astronauts saying they saw it; S6 does not state aid status and S7 is a second-hand relay.
S5 and S8 report unsuccessful attempts without stating aid status.
steps: Verifying an unaided sighting requires a source stating aid status, how the observer identified the Wall, and observation context (C009 v3 section 6).
No source reviewed provides all three for any sighting: S7 states naked eye but is unverified second-hand relay with no identification detail; S6 gives no aid status.
The agency assessments speak to difficulty, and S4 explicitly leaves unaided visibility questionable, so they do not establish that no sighting occurred.
Therefore the predicate is neither established nor refuted by these sources: insufficient_evidence.
inference.not_claimed: No claim that the Wall is never visible unaided from low Earth orbit, that it is easy or usual to see, that any astronaut's report is false, or that a photograph shows naked-eye visibility. No acuity or angular-size calculation is relied on.

excluded_scopes: Q-univ: whether the Wall is never visible unaided from low Earth orbit (C009 v3: not supported, which is not the same as false).
Q-ease and Q-freq: whether it is easy or usual to see (separate predicates; NASA and ESA guidance is attributed context here, not this record's verdict).
Q-exist-rep: whether at least one astronaut has reported seeing it (attributed reports exist with gaps; a separate record if wanted).
Photographic, radar or satellite detection, including long-lens astronaut photography.
limitations: Read gaps (nobody in this review chain read these): the Straits Times original of the Cernan quotation; the CCTV interview footage of Yang Liwei; the book ORBIT; Space.com's original page for S6 (read via NBC's syndicated copy).
